title: The Short Titles Edition
summary: On riots, gaming and the Bank of England.
content:
Mark Slavonia (MJS) is an investor, a pilot, and an avid cyclist. He wrote a two-part WITI about the switch from the Julian to the Gregorian Calendar, which is referenced in this edition. He posts other things that are interesting on his website.

Mark here. A few months ago, I wrote here about the belated adoption of the Gregorian calendar by the United Kingdom in 1753, which was authorized by Parliament through the passage of An Act for Regulating the Commencement of the Year; and for Correcting the Calendar now in Use. In 1892, in a sweeping legislative reform, that Act was renamed, along with many other old laws. It is now simply called the Calendar Act.

Why is this interesting?

The Acts of Parliament go back a long way. Many laws still in force in the United Kingdom predate modern spelling, word usage, capitalization, and naming conventions. Many had florid or grandiloquent titles that might have seemed like a good idea at the time, but became cumbersome and inconvenient to cite again and again.

In 1892, in a feat of pragmatic and effective governance, the British Parliament passed An Act to facilitate the Citation of sundry Acts of Parliament - itself not a terrible name, but the real revolution was found in the Act’s second section:

2. This Act may be cited as the Short Titles Act, 1892.

The Short Titles Act of 1892 then listed and renamed 851 of the most commonly cited and referenced laws in the United Kingdom with new, straightforward, self-explanatory, and brief names.

“An Act for preventing Tumults and riotous Assemblies, and for the more speedy and effectual punishing the Rioters” became The Riot Act.

“An Act to explain, amend, and make more effectual the Laws in being to prevent excessive and deceitful Gaming; and to restrain and prevent the excessive increase of Horse Races” became The Gaming Act.

“An Acte for punishing of divers abuses comitted on the Lord’s Day called Sunday.” became The Sunday Observance Act, 1625.

An Act for granting to theire Majesties severall Rates and Duties upon Tunnage of Shipps and Vessells and upon Beere Ale and other Liquors for secureing certaine Recompenses and Advantages in the said Act mentioned to such Persons as shall voluntarily advance the sume of Fifteene hundred thousand pounde towardd the carrying on the Warr against France became, surprisingly, The Bank Of England Act, 1694.

Quite a few other Sunday Observance Acts and Bank of England Acts are on the list, each designated by their year of enactment.

Here’s one that I particularly like - the original name of the Act was so vague and wordy that they just called it An Act the title whereof begins with the words “An Act to require overseers” and ends with the words “subsequent Acts,” This became The Parish Overseer’s Act, 1802.

The Short Titles Act was such a success that it was followed up in 1896 by a second Short Titles Act, which renamed another 1,000 Acts of Parliament. Subsequent Acts of Parliament generally contain some equivalent of the Short Titles Act’s section two, which designates an official short title for each Act.

It’s hard not to see these new names as an improvement, but I admit that some magic goes out of the world when an Act for punysshement of Pyrotes and Robbers of the See becomes the Sea Offences Act. There’s poetry in an Acte for lymytacon of Accons and for avoyding of Suits in Lawe that is lost in The Limitation Act.

The United States has no direct equivalent of the Short Titles Act. By the time of the formation of the U.S.A., the problem of long titles was understood, and most laws were given short titles from the start.

The full list of old-timey sounding Acts that were renamed can be found in this attached PDF of the Short Titles Act. Take a look at your leisure. I’m sure you’ll find some gems. (MS)
